cards.source_text: More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades. According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging. The Trump administration moved last week to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, citing “outdated restrictions [that] have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities”. Conservationists have criticized the decision. “Our national forests are home to some of America’s most iconic animals, from grizzlies to hellbenders. These forests provide clean drinking water to countless communities. Bulldozing more roads through them will mean dirtier water, fragmented wildlife habitat and greater wildfire risk,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. At-risk species include grizzly bears and gray wolves in the Rocky Mountains, wild salmon in the Pacific north-west and Alaska, Mexican spotted owls and Gila trout in the south-west, as well as rare butterflies and wildflowers nationwide, according to the report. In the Rocky Mountains, 9.7m acres of roadless areas are at risk, including 2.9m acres of critical habitat and nearly 11,000 miles of streams home to 21 imperiled plant and animal species. Montana’s roadless areas also protect watersheds supplying drinking water to communities in Bozeman, the Flathead valley and the Seeley-Swan valley, the report found. In Alaska, the rollback threatens wild salmon in the 9.3m-acre Tongass national forest, which produces more wild salmon than any other national forest. The region’s $1bn-a-year commercial and sport fishing economy which accounts for one in 10 jobs in south-east Alaska may also be affected, the report noted. The Tongass also supplies drinking water to more than a dozen communities, including Sitka, where about 9,000 people rely on the Blue Lake Reservoir. cards.source_text: It’s hard to imagine that the space-crazed general public needed any help getting worked up about astronauts and NASA in the early ’60s. Perhaps the wild popularity of space-related imagery was in part what motivated NASA administrator James Webb to create the NASA Art Program in 1962. Although the program’s handpicked artists weren’t edited or censored in any way, they were briefed on how NASA hoped to be represented, and which emotions their creations were meant to capture—the excitement and uncertainty of exploring these frontiers. NASA was also careful to collect everything the artists produced while participating in the program, from sketches to finished work. In turn, the artists received unprecedented access to launch sites, key personnel, and major events such as Project Mercury and the Apollo 11 Mission. Hundreds of artists, including Andy Warhol, Norman Rockwell, and Laurie Anderson, have brought their unique sensibilities to the project. (Find NASA-inspired art by Warhol and Rockwell above.) (And hey, no shame if you mistakenly assumed Warhol’s 1987 Moonwalk 1 was created as a promo for MTV…) Jamie Wyeth’s 1964 watercolor Gemini Launch Pad includes a humble bicycle, the means by which technicians traveled back and forth between the launch pad and the reinforced-concrete blockhouse where they worked. Photographer Annie Leibovitz offers two views of NASA’s first female pilot and commander, Eileen Collins—with and without helmet. Postage stamp designer, Paul Calle, one of the inaugural group of participating artists, produced a stamp commemorating the Gemini 4 space capsule in celebration of NASA’s 9th anniversary. When the Apollo 11 astronauts suited up prior to blastoff on July 16, 1969, Calle was the only artist present. His quickly rendered felt-tip marker sketches lend a backstage element to the heroic iconography surrounding astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins. One of the items they carried with them on their journey was the engraved printing plate of Calle’s 1967 commemorative stamp. They hand-canceled a proof aboard the flight, on the assumption that post offices might be hard to come by on the moon. In 2016, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory enlisted a team of nine artists, designers, and illustrators to collaborate on 14 posters, a visual throwback to the ones the WPA created between 1938 and 1941 to spark public interest in the National Parks. cards.source_text: It doesn’t quite ring true to call David Bowie a rock star. Ziggy Stardust, the neon synthetic-clad alien alter ego he both created and retired in the early seventies, was, of course, rock stardom outlandishly personified. But then, that was the concept of what turned out to be just one of many personae he deliberately crafted throughout the course of his career. That career was in music, primarily, but looking back on it today, more than a decade after Bowie’s death, it looks more like his medium was culture itself. That’s underscored by his interviews, clips from a variety of which appear in the new video above from YouTube channel T&H Inspiration. Most of T&H’s most popular videos add visuals to speeches by the popularizer of Eastern philosophy Alan Watts, who’s been featured here on Open Culture before. He and Bowie had more in common than it may seem at first, beginning with an Englishness that remained thoroughgoing no matter how far out they ventured into the world. Though Watts’ interest in Buddhism hardly needs stating, it’s worth remembering that he chose to be ordained as an Episcopalian priest rather than as a Buddhist monk. The young Bowie, for his part, very nearly took the latter path, studying under the late Lama Chime Rinpoche, who eventually told him he’d be better off going into the music business. Bowie did so, of course, but with a new “sense of transience and change, which actually became fundamental to my life and my approach to it,” as he put it decades later. That sense manifests even in his early work, but embracing and even pursuing impermanence — the impermanence of sounds, of fashions, of hit records, of life itself — also kept him from getting mired in the irrelevance or auto-kitsch that threatens every superstar. Given the belief that nothing lasts forever, “looking for the source of one’s own being becomes much more important,” as does attempting artistic or intellectual challenges at the very edge of one’s abilities. Alan Watts would probably have agreed. The bigger question is, did he ever hear “Changes”? cards.source_text: As worthy as Dinosaur Jr.’s output has been since their mid-2000s reformation, the group’s work has been tinged with self-consciousness. Where their first three LPs hedged the band’s heroic chops behind ramshackle song structures and slovenly production, post-comeback albums like 2009’s Farm and 2012’s I Bet on Sky buttoned the flannel a bit, mirroring the cleaner, more streamlined sound of their ’90s output, which was mostly J Mascis’ work. By domesticating the Big Muff-induced guitar feedback and leaning into longer songs and the occasional touches of prog, they proved that a bona fide classic-rock trio had been hiding beneath the surface all along. But that polish sometimes gave way to the excessively quirky aimlessness that marked 1997’s Hand It Over before Mascis put Dinosaur Jr. on hiatus. Their last album, 2021’s Sweep It Into Space, maintained the band’s high floor for consistently catchy alt-rock, but its tidy stabs at Kurt Vile-assisted psychedelia sometimes strayed a bit too far from the band’s core of slacker disorder. On There Near, Dinosaur correct course by shedding any self-seriousness they’ve accrued over the past two decades, and instead wallowing happily in the muck of their formative years. Tracked with the same vintage amplifier used on their homemade debut album, the new material is the messiest and most blown-out music they’ve made this side of the millennium. It’s not quite as filth-caked as, say, Bug, but the effortlessness of it recalls the earlier era, prizing poppy melody and immediate self-expression over grandiosity. The best-loved Dinosaur Jr. records intensify the contrast between Mascis’ sheepish vocal demeanor and the raw transparency of the band’s playing, and those two elements are back in optimal sync here. No score yet, be the first to add. The combination is particularly devastating on the bridge of “No Friends,” where Mascis’ groaned admissions of loneliness unfold alongside an ascending guitar lead that sounds as though it’s sobbing in pain. His soloing is particularly creative here (and throughout the album), breaking from his comfort zone to leap high up on the neck and sacrifice wonkiness for emotion. It’s less Guitar Center demo station than half-finished basement. cards.source_text: Every four years, with the reliability of a reelection campaign, Interpol emerge with a new album that sounds remarkably like Interpol. They’re not the kind of band to wade through a murky psychedelia morass for an album-length fuck-you to casual fans, à la MGMT, or douse a long-awaited comeback LP in chintzy pop textures and copious Auto-Tune, like the Strokes just did. When Interpol make a record, they’re all business, and their business is being Interpol, brooding hooks and well-pressed suits and all. They may tweak the formula—the post-punk atmospherics, the alluringly charismatic baritone belonging to Paul Banks, the cryptic lyrics that connote dark emotions but are agile enough to be repurposed for goth tattoos or goofy memes. But they don’t toss it away. That reliability means you can count on them for consistency—aside from the dismal self-titled record, they’ve never made a bad one—but also means it can be tough to differentiate one post-Carlos Interpol album from another. Let’s see: There was the course-correction comeback that reintroduced Interpol as a three-piece, with Banks on bass. There was the surprisingly raw Dave Fridmann production that yielded some strong singles as the band settled into legacy status. There was the remotely written one that, uh, also had a bunch of Interpol songs on it. Now, after hunkering down with another new collaborator (prolific pop producer Andrew Wyatt, not to be confused with rock-dinosaur whisperer Andrew Watt) in their semi-estranged hometown of New York, Interpol return with another scheduled reset. No score yet, be the first to add. By all early signs, This Mirror Weighs a Ton promised a rebirth. It’s Interpol’s first album for Partisan, the thriving indie label that has lately attracted high-profile talent like Beth Orton and PJ Harvey. It’s their first to feature longtime touring bassist Brad Truax, now promoted to an official member. Early press included intriguing mentions of strings, woodwinds, and “experimental sound design” introduced by Wyatt. And its title track, released as a single, was surely the band’s most interesting song in more than a decade: Grainy and haunted, full of wobbly drum loops and gaseous synth clouds, it has a minimalist momentum and a command of empty space that gives Banks’ dour voice newfound authority. cards.source_text: How has Jim James not named an album Wowed Out already? With the classic rock fireworks and cosmic adventures of My Morning Jacket and his solo work alike, the phrase feels so apt that it could almost scan as self-parody. Yet James’ fifth solo album and first in eight years both plays into and thwarts expectations, his boundless voice suggesting it is, in fact, possible to hit capacity. Wielding an array of his wheelhouse sounds with acuity and warmth, James returns with an album whose maybe-goofy-maybe-pensive title allows him to dance between world-weariness and renewed awe, resulting in his best work in a decade. Wowed Out arrives somewhat out of nowhere, following a 2020s thus far spent with the revival of My Morning Jacket after the band nearly collapsed in on itself amid the grueling tours following 2015’s The Waterfall. During something of an unofficial hiatus, James was busy with solo material. Wowed Out originates from a vault of songs he originally worked on in the early ’10s with Brian Reitzell, the former Red Kross drummer, Air collaborator, and composer who provided music for several Sofia Coppola films. With much of the sketches destined for unrealized film scores, they sat untouched until James revisited them in the fall of last year. No score yet, be the first to add. The triumph of My Morning Jacket’s return was relative. For longtime fans, it was a joy to see the band resurrected, reportedly happier and healthier, still leaving scorched earth behind on any stage they visited. Yet the would-be comeback albums of 2021’s self-titled and 2025’s is felt more like ideas of what a My Morning Jacket album should be than My Morning Jacket albums that pushed the envelope the way their best work had. Though not without their highlights, the albums’ often streamlined production yielded a rote sense of attempted grandeur, gesturing at past highs rather than seeking new ones. On Wowed Out, James sounds unburdened even when singing about the weight of the modern world. He moves with subtlety and grace, perhaps liberated from the expectations of MMJ’s resurgence. Wowed Out is a predominantly mellow affair. James’ melodies seem to materialize and unspool, an unforced reclamation of the mystery that once permeated his writing. cards.source_text: Most rappers and beatmakers who manage to stick around for more than a few years, build a dedicated following, and make a healthy living off of music eventually hit a wall. They may ask themselves, “Why am I still doing this?,” searching for the fire they had in their belly when barely anyone knew their name. Music becomes business and business can become tedious. In the background of ii, the long-awaited follow-up to 2020’s Unlocked, Denzel Curry and Kenny Beats—my fault, Kenneth Blume—are reckoning with the reality of the mid-career creative plateau. “I’m not doing this just to do it, I wanna win a Grammy off this hoe,” Curry said in an interview four years ago. “But it feel like I don’t get recognized for what I do, even though I’ve been doing this for a long time.” On “Gone Fishing,” the 31-year-old rapper takes stock of his career trajectory, wide-eyed and full of zeal. He gloats a lil’ bit like he tends to (his passion is “Christ-like,” since 16 he’s been “the zeitgeist”), but what sticks out is how indifferent he’s become about status or stature. “Fuck the best rapper shit, I’m tryna make (cha-ching),” Denzel Curry spits with a shrug. “A history of hits, but for you it’s not hitting.” For the 15 years he’s been around, it feels like the South Florida native has hardly been able to remove the chip on his shoulder, and despite the fact that he says it’s still there, things feel different now. Throughout ii, I can’t shake the feeling that Denzel Curry’s pursuit of contentment (and money) in lieu of industry plaudits has sunk him into creative stasis—his Southern-fried double-time flows and zany one-liners feel tame and predictable, circulating over beats that double down on that feeling. No score yet, be the first to add. Across raps about getting rich and staying rich, Denzel proves he’s still technically proficient, but he’s grown more subdued with time. On the first Unlocked tape with Blume, six years ago, he was growling and barking, channeling DMX cadences as his pitch modulated and distorted. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983). Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex. The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. cards.source_text: A Vocabulary for the Future is a series by the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in which notable thinkers reflect on a word of their choosing and are paired with filmmakers who give their writing a visual interpretation. Together, they invite viewers to see familiar language anew, in the hope of laying the groundwork for a better tomorrow. In this instalment, the American theoretical physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad muses on the nature of touch. Drawing partly on their essay ‘On Touching—The Inhuman That Therefore I Am’ (2012), Barad begins with a puzzle from classical physics: touch, strictly speaking, never happens, since what we feel as contact is only electromagnetic repulsion between atoms that never actually meet. Turning to quantum field theory, they reframe the question entirely. If matter has no stable, self-contained identity – if it is entangled with other matter from the very start – then touch is not a failed meeting between separate bodies, but something already constitutive of what matter is. Paired with visuals by the Barcelona-based digital artist Blanca Rego, the result is a mesmerising set of images that, alongside Barad’s words, turn something as ordinary as touch into a doorway into the deepest questions in physics and philosophy.

cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 41 minute listen ‘A nasty one, the dolphin,’ Derode grumbled when he returned home, trading the humid heat of an Amazonian afternoon for the cool, sheltered interior. Inside, his wife Rosa and I shot hungry looks at his empty hands. Once again, the Caquetá River surrendered no fish. I was only two weeks into my fieldwork with the Andoque people in southern Colombia, and my eyes zigzagged in confusion between the two septuagenarian spouses. What did a dolphin have to do with anything? Rosa explained: ‘Derode had left baits by the river, and it seems a dolphin had stolen the fish that had gotten hooked in them.’ Derode nodded. The fishing had been poor ever since my arrival, and as Rosa cooked lunch from the rice and lentils I had brought from the city – the ‘White People’s Food’ – she reminisced with her husband about times when the river had been generous. She recalled how her grandfather had once hauled in an almost legendary catch by throwing poisonous plants into the shallow stream and asphyxiating the fish in great numbers. Among this enormous catch was a dolphin. Of course, she added, as if it needed no explanation, her grandfather did not eat it. ‘Why not eat the dolphin?’ I asked. The Andoque were accomplished hunters and fishermen, and there was almost no walking, swimming, crawling or flying creature that they wouldn’t relish, if they could catch it. ‘Because dolphins are people,’ Rosa said, matter-of-factly. ‘Besides, their meat smells terrible.’ Dolphins were not simply people, she went on, they were bad people, shapeshifters. Her father had once warned her never to accept the advances of unknown men while bathing at the river. As handsome as they may seem, he had said, they may be dolphins in disguise. Now, look at the photograph above, “Marcel Breuer and His Harem,” by Bauhaus photographer Erich Consemüller, taken sometime around 1927. Except for the fact that Breuer looks more like Ron Mael of Sparks sans mustache than drummer Dee Pop, one might mistake this for a photo of the punk band. This raises a few questions: did art students Bush Tetras look to the women of the Bauhaus for their style? Or did the women of the Bauhaus look to the future and see punk? The second scenario seems more likely since the women of the Bauhaus have not, until recently, been terribly well-known. I personally feel cheated after studying art and art history in college many years ago and only now getting introduced to several significant artists of the radical German art school founded by Walter Gropius. All of its famous exponents and art stars are men, but it seems the gender ratio of the Bauhaus was closer to that of the general population (as was, in many cases, that of the early punk and post-punk scenes). But we don’t tend to learn the names or see the work of these artists, and, in some cases, their work has been posthumously attributed to their male colleagues. Nor are we familiar with their progressive personal style, essential in the Bauhaus’s total approach to revolutionizing the arts, including fashion, as a way to liberate humanity from the dogmas of the past. cards.source_text: The first recreational alligator hunt in Louisiana in more than half a century is about to commence in the swamps of that state, with up to 5,000 hopeful trappers facing strict rules in order to snare a reptile. The state’s fish and wildlife commission banned alligator hunting in 1962 to allow the species to recover after decades of unregulated killings for meat and hides dropped numbers there to below 100,000. Now, with the population above an estimated 3 million in the wild, Louisiana is issuing public permits to licensed hunters for a month-long season beginning 1 October, across eight zones statewide. Although alligator hunting has taken place since an outright 10-year ban ended in 1972, it had been restricted to tightly regulated commercial harvesting, making this the first time the public has been able to legally snare for fun or sport a creature embedded in Louisiana’s culture and history. “Louisiana now has a robust alligator resource capable of providing sustainable recreational harvest opportunities to Louisiana residents without negatively impacting a highly valuable commercial industry that provides more than $250m annually to Louisiana’s economy,” the Louisiana department of wildlife and fisheries (LWF) said in a statement accompanying details of the hunt. Applicants have until Monday to enter a lottery for up to two per person of 5,000 tags that will allow them to hunt an alligator, with state residents paying $25 and visitors $150 for each zone they visit, on top of a $50 application fee. The hunt has been designated strictly non-commercial, meaning that those who trap one cannot sell the meat or skin. Applicants must already possess a basic hunting license issued by LWF, and are restricted to hook and line trapping, meaning they cannot use poles or other methods favored by poachers. Firearms can only be used to kill captured alligators, not for shooting free-swimming reptiles. The hunt brings Louisiana broadly into line with Florida, another state that said its conservation programs allowed alligator numbers to recover to the point where recreational hunting is permitted. Florida introduced a similarly regulated statewide program in 1988.

All seven were from Kalipety village in the Tenondé Porã Indigenous Territory in São Paulo state. A fisher who witnessed the crash told police that the corn-filled cargo trailer detached from the truck and “violently” struck the passenger car, according to a police report seen by Mongabay. The force of the collision caused both vehicles to catch fire, killing everyone in the car and incinerating the bodies. The truck driver fled the scene of the accident, the witness said. The bodies have not yet been officially identified but community members confirmed that the victims were Karaí Tiago Honório dos Santos, 34; his wife, Kerexu Laudiceia Benites, also a community leader, 31; their children, Jaxuka Luna Benites Santos, 7, and Tadeu Hiago Werá Mirim Benites dos Santos, 14; his sister, Kerexu Cleonice Honório dos Santos, 42; Ileo Benites, 32; and Genilson Euzébio Karay Mirim, 30. Karaí Tiago Honório dos Santos was the executive coordinator of the Guarani Yvyrupa Commission and Guarani Inter-Village Committee, where he worked to further the rights of the Guarani and other Indigenous peoples in Brazil. He also spearheaded environmental recovery and agrobiodiversity efforts. “[Tiago’s] journey was interrupted in such a brutal way, and what a sad coincidence that [it was] by a truck loaded with corn.” Tatiane Klein, an anthropologist and friend of Karaí Tiago who worked with him for more than a decade, told Mongabay by phone. “They were going to Mato Grosso do Sul to visit relatives and exchange traditional seeds that they cultivate in the Kalipety [Guarani village].” According to Klein, he was a serious and generous leader with a collective approach to his leadership, often pushing others to speak and training younger leaders. items.summary: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off? In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983). Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex. items.title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?
items.summary: Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needs The UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse. In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle. Continue reading...

items.title: How to make a bestseller: insiders reveal the tricks of the book trade
items.summary: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumn Think about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, a TikTok video? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta? The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. And, more recently, persuasion often comes from BookTokers and online influencers, social media videos, podcasts and Instagram posts. How is all this changing publishing? Continue reading...

items.title: Trump rollback of US forest protections could accelerate extinction of 400 endangered species
items.summary: Decision to rescind ‘roadless rule’ opens more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades. According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging.
